debate.situation: You are asking why places like Bergen, Dublin or London have mild winters while parts of Canada at similar latitudes, such as Labrador or Hudson Bay, are far colder. The familiar answer is the Gulf Stream, but it is less clear how much of the difference the ocean explains and how much the winds and land explain. The decisive uncertainty is how the warmth is shared out between ocean currents, prevailing winds, and the heat the Atlantic stores up over the summer.

minds.title: The Ocean Voyager
minds.concern: Follow the water: warm currents carry heat north and deliver it to coasts.
minds.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
minds.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea

minds.title: The Conveyor Engineer
minds.concern: Look at the whole circulation: how heat moves in the deep and surface ocean, and what happens if that circulation changes.
minds.author: Wallace Broecker

minds.title: The Atmosphere Physicist
minds.concern: Test the story with energy budgets: winds, seasons and a heat-storing ocean may matter more than any one current.
minds.author: Raymond Pierrehumbert

debate.speaker: The Ocean Voyager
debate.text: Start with the obvious: a river of warm water flows from the tropics up past Norway, and Norway's coast stays ice-free in winter. The Labrador coast gets cold water from the north instead. Same latitude, opposite currents. The sea is the difference.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855), Gulf Stream discussion; source not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Nice story, but check the arithmetic. Ocean currents carry heat, yes, but over the whole North Atlantic the air carries a lot too. And in winter Europe is warmed by air that has just crossed open ocean. Which one is doing the warming, current or wind?
debate.author: Raymond Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: [Basis: Raymond Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate, chapters on atmospheric heat transport; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Ocean Voyager
debate.text: Fair, the wind matters. But why is the air that arrives so mild? Because it passed over water the current kept warm. You cannot split them. Take away my current and your winds arrive over colder sea, and Europe feels it.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855); source not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Engineer
debate.text: I'll back Maury partway. The Atlantic is unusual: its circulation sends warm surface water north, where it cools, sinks and returns deep. That moves a huge amount of heat. I'd go further than my own book, though: how much of Europe's mildness this explains is still argued.
debate.author: Wallace Broecker
debate.basis: [Basis: Wallace Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: That's the problem with the conveyor as a headline. Take the Pacific: it has no comparable overturning, yet Alaska and British Columbia are also mild compared with Siberia. If the conveyor were the main cause, the Pacific coast should look like Labrador. It doesn't.
debate.author: Raymond Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: [Basis: Raymond Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Engineer
debate.text: Good counterexample, and it narrows my claim. The Pacific coast is warmed by westerly winds off a large ocean. So the conveyor isn't the whole story. Still, the Atlantic is warmer at high latitudes than the Pacific, and I think the circulation is part of why.
debate.author: Wallace Broecker
debate.basis: [Basis: Wallace Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Then here's the piece neither of you has named. Water holds heat far better than land. The ocean soaks up summer sun and releases it slowly through winter, while a continental interior cools fast. Winds from west to east deliver that stored warmth to the west coast of a continent.
debate.author: Raymond Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: [Basis: Raymond Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Ocean Voyager
debate.text: That explains why Vancouver is mild, and I accept it. But Canada's east coast sits downwind of land, so the westerlies arrive already chilled. Europe gets ocean air; Labrador gets Canadian winter. My current and your winds are the same argument seen from two decks.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: [Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea (1855); source not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Physicist
debate.text: Not quite the same argument. They make different predictions. If the current were the main cause, shutting it down would chill Europe a lot. If winds and stored heat dominate, the chill would be milder. That is something we can ask models to test.
debate.author: Raymond Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: [Basis: Raymond Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate; section not verified, no link given]

debate.speaker: The Conveyor Engineer
debate.text: And that is why it matters beyond curiosity. Even if the conveyor is not the main cause, it is the part that could change. I'd say wind and stored heat set the baseline, and the circulation determines how much extra warmth Europe gets on top.
debate.author: Wallace Broecker
debate.basis: [Basis: Wallace Broecker, The Great Ocean Conveyor; section not verified, no link given]

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the question is really about three linked things: the ocean stores heat, westerly winds carry it eastward onto west-facing coasts, and the Atlantic's circulation adds extra warmth at high latitudes. The 'Gulf Stream warms Europe' story is partly right but oversimplified. What remains disputed is how much each contributes, and especially how large the extra contribution from the Atlantic circulation is. A possible reflection: when you hear a one-cause explanation of a climate pattern, what comparison case (such as the Pacific coast) would test it? Note that the sources here could not be checked online, so the book references are attributions of well-known ideas, not verified citations.
debate.dependsOn: If you want the simple answer, it is: warm ocean water plus prevailing westerly winds bring mild maritime air to Europe, while eastern Canada gets cold continental air. If the question is why Europe is milder than the Pacific comparison would suggest, the Atlantic circulation becomes more relevant. If the question is what would happen if the circulation weakened, the competing explanations predict different sizes of cooling, which can be separated by comparing climate model experiments and by comparing Atlantic and Pacific west coasts at the same latitude.
